summary: Describes the architecture of SNMP management frameworks. It is modular: an SNMP engine made of a message processing subsystem, a security subsystem and an access control subsystem, plus one or more applications that sit on top of the engine. This lets the protocol evolve without redoing everything.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3411 is a blueprint for SNMP that splits the system into separate parts for sending messages, checking security, deciding access and running applications. Each part can be swapped out without rebuilding the whole system.

questions: what are the parts of an snmp engine
what are the snmpv3 security levels
subtitle: A modular blueprint that splits SNMP into swappable parts: an engine, message processing, security, access control and applications.

tldr.problem: SNMP had grown through several versions with weak security for set operations, and each upgrade risked disturbing the whole framework.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3411 defines a modular layout with an SNMP engine (dispatcher plus message processing, security and access control subsystems) and applications on top, joined by abstract service interfaces.
tldr.outcome: Parts such as message formats or security models can be replaced without redoing the rest. It is an Internet Standard (STD 62), obsoletes RFC 2571, and has been updated by RFC 5343 and RFC 5590.

facts.label: Engine parts
facts.value: Dispatcher, message processing, security, access control

today: RFC 3411 is an Internet Standard (STD 62) and has not been obsoleted. It has been updated by RFC 5343 and RFC 5590. It replaced RFC 2571.

sections.title: Purpose of the Architecture
sections.content:
RFC 3411 defines a vocabulary and an architecture for describing SNMP management frameworks. It does not give a general introduction to SNMP or a history of it; instead it sets out a modular structure so that parts of SNMP can evolve without redoing everything.

The goals include reusing earlier work, addressing the need for secure SET support (called the most important deficiency in SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c), keeping SNMP simple and cheap to implement in minimal form, and making it possible to upgrade portions without disrupting an entire framework.

An SNMP management system has nodes with SNMP entities that answer commands and send notifications (traditionally called agents), at least one entity that issues commands or receives notifications (traditionally called a manager), and a management protocol between them.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sets out the parts of an SNMP system and how they fit together. This lets each part be improved without replacing the whole system.

sections.title: Modular Design
sections.content:
The architecture defines subsystems as abstract services and abstract service interfaces as the boundaries between them. Each subsystem specification is meant to be self-contained so that different portions can move along the standards track independently.

The modularity applies to specifications, not necessarily to implementations. The RFC requires that security and access control parameters be remotely configurable since secrets need frequent changes. It also aims to keep complexity low so simple devices can use few resources.

A subsystem is an abstract, incomplete specification. A model is a specific, implementable design of a subsystem. An implementation instantiates a subsystem conforming to one or more models.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece has a clear job. The rules describe what connects them, but not how to build them. This keeps simple systems simple while allowing larger ones to be more capable.

sections.title: The SNMP Entity and Engine
sections.content:
An SNMP entity is an implementation of the architecture consisting of one SNMP engine plus one or more applications. The engine is identified by a unique snmpEngineID within an administrative domain.

The engine has four parts: the Dispatcher (one per engine), which sends and receives messages, determines the message version, and hands PDUs to the right Message Processing Model; the Message Processing Subsystem, which prepares outgoing messages and extracts data from incoming ones using one or more Message Processing Models (such as SNMPv3); the Security Subsystem, which provides authentication and privacy using one or more Security Models (such as USM); and the Access Control Subsystem, which provides authorization using one or more Access Control Models.

Applications sit on top and include command generators, command responders, notification originators, notification receivers and proxy forwarders. An entity with command generators or notification receivers is traditionally called a manager; one with command responders or notification originators is traditionally called an agent.
sections.plainLanguage: The engine is the core that routes messages. Four desks handle sorting, envelope work, identity checks and access decisions. The applications are the programs that send and receive the actual commands and notifications.

sections.title: Naming and Contexts
sections.content:
The architecture names three kinds of things: entities, identities and management information. A principal is the who on whose behalf services are provided. A securityName is a human-readable, model-independent string representing a principal. Security Models map between security names and their model-specific representations.

For management information, an SNMP context is a collection of management information accessible by an SNMP entity. The same item of information can exist in more than one context. A context is identified by a contextEngineID and a contextName, and each contextName must be unique within an entity. A scopedPDU holds a contextEngineID, a contextName and a PDU.

To identify one item you need the engine ID, the context name, the object type and the instance.
sections.plainLanguage: A user has a name. The data is organized into separate contexts, like different workspaces. To find one piece of data, you need to know which engine, which context, which object, and which instance.

sections.title: Abstract Service Interfaces
sections.content:
Section 4 defines primitives for abstract service interfaces between subsystems. These describe externally observable behavior, not APIs or implementation requirements.

The Dispatcher provides primitives such as sendPdu, processPdu, returnResponsePdu, processResponsePdu, plus registerContextEngineID and unregisterContextEngineID. The Message Processing Subsystem provides prepareOutgoingMessage, prepareResponseMessage and prepareDataElements. The Security Subsystem provides generateRequestMsg, processIncomingMsg and generateResponseMsg. The Access Control Subsystem provides isAccessAllowed.

When a command is sent, the Dispatcher asks the Message Processing Model to prepare it, which in turn asks the Security Model to secure it. Responses flow back through the same path to the application.
sections.plainLanguage: Each part offers a small set of requests to other parts, like asking a desk to wrap, check, or decide. This keeps the pieces loosely connected.

sections.title: Registries and Numbering
sections.content:
Section 6 creates three IANA-managed number spaces. Security models are numbered 0 to 255, with 0 reserved for "any", 1 for SNMPv1, 2 for SNMPv2c, and 3 for the User-Based Security Model (USM). Message processing models are numbered 0 to 255, with 0 for SNMPv1, 1 for SNMPv2c, 2 for SNMPv2u and SNMPv2*, and 3 for SNMPv3. SnmpEngineID formats assign values to the fifth octet, with IANA managing values 6 to 127.

Section 5 defines the SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB for instrumenting entities. PDUs are classified by function (Read, Write, Response, Notification, Internal) and by whether a response is expected (Confirmed, Unconfirmed).
sections.plainLanguage: Numbers are assigned so different implementations agree on what each number means, like which lock type or which message style is being used.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Three securityLevel values are defined, ordered from weakest to strongest: noAuthNoPriv (no authentication, no privacy), authNoPriv (authentication without privacy) and authPriv (authentication with privacy). Every message has a security level, and all subsystems and applications must supply a value or abide by the supplied one.

Security Models should protect against modification of information and masquerade, and against message stream modification (reordering, delay or replay beyond what the network does) and disclosure. They need not protect against denial of service or traffic analysis.

The MIB module defined in this RFC has no writable objects. Implementations must protect configuration secrets, and applications should take reasonable steps to protect data from disclosure.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages can be unsigned and unsealed, signed only, or signed and sealed. The focus is on keeping messages honest and private, not on stopping someone from blocking traffic entirely.
